captions.instagram:
How does an extension board work?

Inside every extension board are just three strips of brass. Plug in a kettle, an iron and a heater and watch 20 amps squeeze through a cord made for 6, see why a coiled reel cooks, and find out what a spike guard really guards against.

→ Inside an extension board there are just three strips of brass: live, neutral and earth.
→ The earth pin is longer, so it connects first and opens the child shutters.
→ Every socket gets the full 230 volts, and every appliance adds its own current to the bar.
→ A kettle, an iron and a heater together pull about 20 amps through a cord made for 6.
→ A cord is a long thin resistor: double the current and it makes four times the heat.

youtubeLong.title: How does an extension board work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Inside every extension board are just three strips of brass. Plug in a kettle, an iron and a heater and watch 20 amps squeeze through a cord made for 6, see why a coiled reel cooks, and find out what a spike guard really guards against.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/extensionboardclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/extensionboardclear

In this video:
• Three strips of brass. Inside the board, three brass bus bars run its whole length: live, neutral and earth.
• Everything in parallel. Every socket gets the full 230 V, and each appliance draws its own current, I = P ÷ V.
• Why cords get hot. A cord is a long, thin resistor: about 0.026 Ω per metre in each core of a 0.75 mm² cord.
• The wall MCB does not guard the cord. The board's own fuse or bimetal breaker follows a time-current curve: minutes for a small overload, a blink for a big one.
• Spikes and the third pin. A spike guard's blue disc is a varistor.
• Read the label, not the name. An extension board is sockets on a cord.
